item.title: Exploring GraphDB and Neo4j - A Guide to Graph Databases
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Exploring GraphDB and Neo4j
#

Table row vs graph — three contrasts
#

A relational row stores one record; you join tables when a question crosses entities. A graph stores nodes (entities) and relationships (edges) so a path query follows links directly.

Relational table Graph (Neo4j)
What you store One row = one record with columns One node = entity with labels and properties
How links work Foreign keys; the database joins at query time Relationships are stored on the graph and traversed hop by hop
Natural question “All rows where country = 'IN'” “Who is two hops from Alice on :KNOWS?”

One Cypher pattern that reads relationships (friends-of-friends):

MATCH (alice:Person {name: 'Alice'})-[:KNOWS*2]->(fof:Person)
RETURN DISTINCT fof.name

Neo4j is one graph database; GraphDB (Ontotext) is another product with RDF/SPARQL — this article compares graph ideas to SQL and walks Neo4j Cypher in depth below.

item.title: Type of Databases
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
What are the various types of databases?
#

Introduction
#

In the 21st Century, Data is the real oil of machines. There are different kinds of oils and there are different kinds of containers. Similarly, there are different kinds of data and there are different kinds of database software to manage these databases. Broadly we call them SQL and NoSQL databases. But In the NoSQL, there are some other finer groups for specific purposes. For how those database types fit into lakes, warehouses, lakehouses, and marts at enterprise scale, see Data Lake vs Data Warehouse vs Data Mart vs Lakehouse. Let’s look into these.
